site.title: Teuchi Udon
site.tagline: Udon kneaded, rolled and cut by hand every morning, in a small shop on Mugi Lane.

posts.title: New wheat from the hill farms
posts.excerpt: Twelve sacks, one small mill and a dough that needs less water.
posts.content:
Every October the farms on the hills send down their spring wheat, milled slowly at the small mill by the river. This year it came a week early, pale and fine.

New flour drinks less water, so for the first month we cut the salt water by a ladle. The noodles come out a little softer and taste sweeter, which the regulars notice at once.

posts.title: Why we still use well water
posts.excerpt: The kelp opens slowly in soft water, and the noodles keep their shine.
posts.content:
The well behind the shop is older than the shop. Its water is soft and cool all year, and the kelp we soak in it overnight gives up its taste without turning bitter.

We also rinse the boiled noodles in it. Cold, soft water firms the surface quickly, so a zaru bowl stays glossy from the kitchen to the counter.

posts.title: The first curry day of the year
posts.excerpt: When the morning is cold enough to see your breath, the aprons come out.
posts.content:
We do not choose the date. The first morning the window by the board fogs over, Nao writes curry udon on the slate and we take the cotton aprons out of the cupboard.

The curry is made from the same dashi as every other bowl, so it is gentle rather than hot. Most people finish it with a spoon, and a few ask for rice to wipe the bowl clean.
